title: Sadhna's plea for grace
hookLine: Sadhna, remembered as a butcher, pleads to be saved by grace (Bilaval, Sadhna, ang 858)

lines: A BOAT AFTER THE SWIMMER DROWNS.
cards: A lifeguard waits until the swimmer has gone under for good, then rows out with a boat. What use is that? Sadhna asks almost exactly that question, out loud, to God.
Tradition remembers him as a butcher, and his hymn sits in the Guru Granth Sahib all the same. It isn't calm. It's urgent, a little bold, and full of arguments.
He isn't asking whether grace exists. He's asking for it now.

teach.b: Sadhna's hymn is in Raag Bilaval, on Ang 858, and he argues like someone who knows he can't earn what he's asking for. First, in paraphrase: O Guru of the world, what good are Your virtues if my karma isn't wiped away?
Why run to a lion for shelter, if a jackal is going to eat you anyway? The point of refuge is that it's stronger than what's chasing you.
Second, the chaatrik, the rainbird of Indian poetry that longs for a single raindrop. For one drop, the bird suffers; once its life is gone, an ocean is no use to it.

teach.h: A BOAT AFTER DROWNING IS NO USE.
teach.b: Third, the boat. My life is worn out and unsteady, he says; how can I wait? If I drown and die, and then a boat arrives, tell me, who will you put on board?
Each picture says the same thing from a new side: grace that comes too late isn't grace. Then everything drops away.

teach.h: I HAVE NOTHING; SAVE ME NOW.
teach.b: In paraphrase: I am nothing, I have nothing, nothing at all is mine. At this moment, protect my honor; Sadhna is Your servant. That's the plea.
Not a list of good deeds, because he doesn't claim any. Just empty hands and a deadline. Sikh teaching speaks of nadar, the gracious glance of the Lord, which no one can force or buy.
Sadhna's hymn is what asking for that glance sounds like when there's nothing left to bargain with.

how: Sadhna's hymn is sung in gurdwaras as part of the Guru Granth Sahib, and Sikh teaching speaks of nadar, the Lord's gracious glance, as a gift that can be asked for but never earned or forced.

o: a vow to fast until a prayer is answered
the Lord's gracious glance, never forced or bought
a reward earned by a long life of good deeds

p: why seek its shelter if the jackal eats you
longs for one drop of water

s: Sadhna lists his good deeds to earn grace
he says: I am nothing, I have nothing, nothing at all is mine.
Sadhna's hymn is calm and patient
it's urgent: if a boat comes after I drown, who will you put on board?
Sadhna compares himself to a rainbird longing for one drop
for one drop the rainbird suffers; once its life is gone, an ocean is no use.

games.q: you're Sadhna, asking for grace, and you know your record won't save you. what do you bring?
o: a promise to do better later.
empty hands: I have nothing; save me now.
games.why: he brings nothing: I am nothing, I have nothing, nothing is mine. at this moment, protect my honor.

practice: Find the place where effort has run out: a habit you can't break, a relationship you can't fix, a fear you can't argue away.

Don't make a case for yourself; if you pray, ask once, simply, for grace there, and if you don't, just name it honestly, once, with empty hands like Sadhna's. Then breathe, with Waheguru on each breath out if you like.

wordCard.voice: Nadar. The gracious glance of the Lord, which no one can force or buy: Sadhna's plea when there was nothing left to bargain with.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: the gracious glance, the Sikh word for grace that can't be forced or bought.

carryVoice: Your line: saved by grace. A boat after the drowning is no use, so Sadhna asks now. Seven hundred eighty-five days, and counting.

sources.ref: Bilaval, Sadhna (nrip kanniaa ke kaarnai), Ang 858
